nodes.text: ASR systems trained on single-distribution data fail to generalize, making far more errors than humans outside their training domain.
Reliable general-purpose speech recognition is necessary for real-world deployment; brittle models require expensive re-training per application domain.
Unsupervised pre-training (e.g., Wav2Vec 2.0) scales to 1M hours and improves audio encoders, but requires supervised fine-tuning that reintroduces distributional brittleness.
Multi-domain supervised training increases robustness, but existing efforts combine at most ~5,000 hours of high-quality labeled audio.
Weakly supervised training on large noisy datasets dramatically improves robustness in computer vision, suggesting the same may hold for speech.
Weakly supervised speech recognition has not been scaled past ~30,000 hours, leaving untested whether the scale needed for robust zero-shot generalization is achievable.
RQ1: Does scaling weakly supervised pretraining to 680,000 hours produce zero-shot transfer that matches or exceeds supervised models on diverse speech benchmarks?
RQ2: Does a single model trained with a multitask token format generalize across transcription, translation, voice activity detection, and language identification?
RQ3: How do model scale and data scale affect performance?
RQ4: Does joint multilingual/multitask training help or hurt compared to English-only training?

Whisper: an encoder-decoder Transformer trained via next-token prediction on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet audio across five model sizes (39M to 1,550M parameters), using a token-based multitask format.
Zero-shot evaluation on 13 academic ASR datasets spanning diverse domains; comparison with supervised LibriSpeech models matched on in-distribution performance.
Zero-shot Whisper (2.7% WER on LibriSpeech clean) achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over a supervised model with the same in-distribution WER on 13 other datasets.
Whisper robustness frontier includes the 95% CI of human robustness; English ASR approaches human accuracy on Kincaid46.
Multitask token format enables competitive zero-shot performance on translation (29.1 BLEU CoVoST2 overall SOTA) and functional language ID (80.3% on overlapping languages).
Performance scales with model size across multilingual SR, translation, and language ID; English SR saturates at large scale.
Performance improves monotonically with training data from 3,405 to 681,070 hours across all tasks.
Joint multilingual/multitask training causes negative transfer at small model scales but positive transfer at large scales.
The robustness gap between ASR and human performance is primarily a training distribution problem, not a capacity problem; diverse supervised coverage is the key driver.

Whisper demonstrates that scaling weakly supervised pretraining with diverse internet data to 680k hours achieves human-like robustness and zero-shot generalization for a single multitask speech model.
Fine-tuning not evaluated; low-resource language performance remains poor; text normalizer developed alongside model; human comparison uses small sample.

Zero-shot evaluation should be emphasized alongside in-distribution evaluation to avoid overstating ASR capabilities; large-scale weakly supervised pretraining is a viable path for robust speech recognition.
Better decoding for long-form transcription, targeted data collection for low-resource languages, fine-tuning studies, and language model integration remain open.
